notes.kkumi-na-emu: Onze: one of the six numbers from 11 to 16 with its own name.
notes.abiri: Vingt: the -t is silent, except in vingt-deux, vingt-trois…
notes.lukumi: Mille, never un mille, and never with -s.
notes.kya-bbeeyi: Cher for a masculine noun, chère for a feminine one.
notes.kendeezaako: To a stranger, the polite form is Baissez un peu le prix.
notes.sabini: Soixante-dix in France; septante in Belgium and DR Congo.

guidebook.intro: French numbers are regular up to sixty, then they start doing sums. You’ll also learn to ask the price and bargain politely.

tips.title: Eleven to nineteen
body: From 11 to 16 the numbers have their own names: **onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize**. From 17 they add up: **dix-sept** (ten-seven), **dix-huit, dix-neuf**.
The tens: **vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante**. Add the units with a hyphen: **vingt-deux, trente-cinq**, but say **et un** for one: **vingt et un**.

tips.title: Seventy, eighty, ninety
body: In France, 70 is **soixante-dix** (sixty-ten), 80 is **quatre-vingts** (four-twenties) and 90 is **quatre-vingt-dix** (four-twenty-ten). So 75 is **soixante-quinze** and 99 is **quatre-vingt-dix-neuf**.
Belgium, Switzerland and the Democratic Republic of Congo often say **septante** (70) and **nonante** (90) instead, and the Swiss say **huitante** for 80.

tips.title: C’est combien ?
body: To ask the price: **C’est combien ?** or **Combien coûte ceci ?** To bargain, ask the seller to lower the price: **Vous pouvez baisser un peu ?** When you agree: **D’accord, je le prends.**
**Cent** (100) and **mille** (1,000) don’t take **un**: **cent shillings, mille shillings**. **Mille** never takes an -s: **cinq mille**.

culture.title: Francs CFA and other money
body: Fourteen countries in West and Central Africa share the **franc CFA**; Congo, Rwanda and Burundi each have their own franc. Prices are often in thousands, so **mille** is a word you’ll hear a lot.
